cards.lead: Atomism in the Vaisheshika school of India
cards.note: The lead's date c. 500-100 BCE is not in the source: the Stanford entry says only that the origins are 'several centuries before the common era'. The same entry says Greek-influence claims are uncommon in recent scholarship, which points away from borrowing but does not state independence, so origin is unknown. Impact depth and generativity kept at the lead's values.
cards.name: Atomic theory in the Vaisheshika school, India
cards.summary: The Vaisheshika school argued that all matter is made of eternal, indivisible atoms that combine into larger bodies, c. several centuries before the common era.
cards.description: Vaisheshika thinkers in classical India, traditionally credited to Kanada, held that matter is built from indivisible atoms that combine into dyads and triads before forming perceptible bodies. The Stanford Encyclopedia says atomism in this school probably began several centuries before the common era, and it was developed in dialogue with other Indian schools.
cards.origin_note: The entry notes that claims of Greek influence are uncommon in recent scholarship, but it does not say the Indian atomism was reached without knowledge of Greek theory, so independence is not established.

impact.note: Kept from the lead. The entry documents sustained debate between Nyaya-Vaisheshika, Buddhist and Jaina atomism, which supports reach and generativity of 1 but not more.

events.label: several centuries before the common era
events.statement: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy says the origins of atomism in classical Indian philosophy likely lie several centuries before the common era.
events.quote: The beginnings of atomism in classical Indian philosophy are difficult to ascertain, but it likely has origins several centuries before the common era.
events.locator: Section 1, Atomism in Classical Indian Philosophy

open_questions: The Vaisheshika Sutra's date is not settled in the fetched sources. Web pages give ranges from the 6th to the 2nd century BCE, but none was a scholarly source that could be opened, so the lead's c. 500-100 BCE is unsupported.
Halbfass (1992) and Ganeri's accounts of the Greek-influence question were not reached; the independence question needs them.
Keith (1921) argued for Greek influence and is cited by the entry; his argument was not checked.

cards.note: The Paris discovery of uranium radiation in 1896 and the Curies' 1898 work are confirmed. The 1902 Rutherford and Soddy account was worked out at McGill University in Montreal, not Paris, so it is a separate place. Generativity lowered to 2: the fetched sources document the decay theory and the radiation types, but not the later fields the lead names.
cards.name: Discovery of radioactivity, Paris
cards.summary: Henri Becquerel found in 1896 that uranium emits invisible rays, and Pierre and Marie Curie found further radioactive materials in 1898, opening the study of atomic change.
cards.description: In Paris in 1896 Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts emit invisible rays that fog photographic plates, a property the sources describe as coming from the uranium itself. In November 1898 Pierre and Marie Curie reported two highly radioactive materials separated from pitchblende. In 1902 Ernest Rutherford and Frederick Soddy, working in Montreal, reached an account of radioactivity as the spontaneous change of one kind of atom into another.
cards.origin_note: The sources name Becquerel's 1896 observation in Paris as the discovery and cite no earlier observation of spontaneous radiation from a substance.

impact.note: Generativity lowered from the lead's 3: the sources document the decay theory and radiation types, not the later dating, medical and energy uses, which were not checked.

events.statement: Henri Becquerel discovered that uranium emits radiation, reported to the French Academy of Sciences in Paris in 1896.
events.quote: The radioactivity of uranium was discovered in 1896 by Henri Becquerel who, starting from a wrong idea, progressively realized what he was observing

events.label: November 1898
events.statement: In November 1898 Pierre and Marie Curie reported the chemical separation of two highly radioactive materials from pitchblende.
events.quote: In November 1898, they reported the chemical separation of two unknown materials from the ore pitchblende, both highly radioactive

events.statement: In 1902 Rutherford and Soddy reached a picture of radioactive atoms decaying into other atoms, working at McGill in Montreal.
events.quote: Rutherford and Soddy came rather quickly (in 1902) to a picture of this type

open_questions: The date 24 February 1896 for Becquerel's first note (Comptes rendus 122, p. 420) is given by a secondary paper (arXiv 2412.14882, Stokes letter) and a Wikipedia-derived date of 27 February was seen in search; check the Comptes rendus volume directly.
The 1901-1902 thorium work of Rutherford and Soddy may merit its own record, as the lead suggests.
Later uses (radiometric dating, radiotherapy, nuclear energy) are not yet sourced in these cards.
